questions.q: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}\) for \(x>0\), given \(y=6\) when \(x=2\).
questions.answer: Separate: \(\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}\). Integrate: \(\ln|y|=\ln|x|+C\), so \(y=Ax\). Using \(y=6,x=2\): \(A=3\). Solution: \(y=3x\).
questions.explanation: Separate: \(\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}\). Integrate: \(\ln|y|=\ln|x|+C\), so \(y=Ax\). Using \(y=6,x=2\): \(A=3\). Solution: \(y=3x\).

questions.q: The rate of decrease of a quantity \(Q\) is proportional to \(Q\) itself. Write a differential equation for \(\frac{dQ}{dt}\), using \(k>0\) as the constant of proportionality.
questions.target: Forming differential equations from a description
questions.answer: \(\frac{dQ}{dt}=-kQ\).
questions.explanation: \(\frac{dQ}{dt}=-kQ\).

questions.q: A tank drains so that the rate of decrease of its volume \(V\) is proportional to \(\sqrt{V}\). Write a differential equation for \(\frac{dV}{dt}\), using \(k>0\).
questions.target: Forming differential equations from a description
questions.answer: \(\frac{dV}{dt}=-k\sqrt{V}\).
questions.explanation: \(\frac{dV}{dt}=-k\sqrt{V}\).

questions.q: A chemical reaction's concentration \(C\) decreases at a rate proportional to the square of the concentration. Write a differential equation for \(\frac{dC}{dt}\), using \(k>0\).
questions.target: Forming differential equations from a description
questions.answer: \(\frac{dC}{dt}=-kC^2\).
questions.explanation: \(\frac{dC}{dt}=-kC^2\).

questions.q: A population \(P\) satisfies \(\frac{dP}{dt}=0.08P\). If \(P=500\) when \(t=0\), find \(P\) when \(t=10\), to the nearest whole number.

questions.q: Solve \(\frac{dV}{dt}=-k\sqrt{V}\) (from the tank problem above), given \(V(0)=V_0\).
questions.target: Solving modeling equations with initial conditions
questions.answer: Separate: \(V^{-1/2}\,dV=-k\,dt\). Integrate: \(2\sqrt{V}=-kt+C\). Using \(V(0)=V_0\): \(C=2\sqrt{V_0}\). So \(\sqrt{V}=\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\), giving \(V(t)=\left(\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\right)^2\).
questions.explanation: Separate: \(V^{-1/2}\,dV=-k\,dt\). Integrate: \(2\sqrt{V}=-kt+C\). Using \(V(0)=V_0\): \(C=2\sqrt{V_0}\). So \(\sqrt{V}=\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\), giving \(V(t)=\left(\sqrt{V_0}-\frac{kt}{2}\right)^2\).

questions.q: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}+3y=12\) using an integrating factor, given \(y=2\) when \(x=0\).
questions.target: First-order linear differential equations using an integrating factor
questions.answer: Integrating factor: \(e^{3x}\). \(\frac{d}{dx}(ye^{3x})=12e^{3x}\). Integrate: \(ye^{3x}=4e^{3x}+C\), so \(y=4+Ce^{-3x}\). Using \(y=2,x=0\): \(C=-2\). Solution: \(y=4-2e^{-3x}\).
questions.explanation: Integrating factor: \(e^{3x}\). \(\frac{d}{dx}(ye^{3x})=12e^{3x}\). Integrate: \(ye^{3x}=4e^{3x}+C\), so \(y=4+Ce^{-3x}\). Using \(y=2,x=0\): \(C=-2\). Solution: \(y=4-2e^{-3x}\).

questions.answer: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=6e^{2x}\). Substituting: \(6e^{2x}-2(3e^{2x})=6e^{2x}-6e^{2x}=0\), confirming the equation is satisfied.

questions.q: Verify that \(y=x^2+Ce^{-x}\) is a general solution of \(\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x^2+2x\).
questions.answer: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-Ce^{-x}\). Substituting: \((2x-Ce^{-x})+(x^2+Ce^{-x})=2x+x^2\), which matches the right-hand side \(x^2+2x\) exactly, confirming the equation is satisfied for any constant \(C\).
questions.explanation: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-Ce^{-x}\). Substituting: \((2x-Ce^{-x})+(x^2+Ce^{-x})=2x+x^2\), which matches the right-hand side \(x^2+2x\) exactly, confirming the equation is satisfied for any constant \(C\).

questions.q: Find the general solution of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=4x^3-6x\), and explain what determines a particular solution from this family.
questions.answer: Integrating directly: \(y=x^4-3x^2+C\). A particular solution is obtained by specifying one point that the curve must pass through, which fixes the value of the arbitrary constant \(C\).
questions.explanation: Integrating directly: \(y=x^4-3x^2+C\). A particular solution is obtained by specifying one point that the curve must pass through, which fixes the value of the arbitrary constant \(C\).

questions.q: A cup of tea at \(85^\circ\)C is placed in a room at \(22^\circ\)C. Using \(T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}\), and given that after 8 minutes the tea has cooled to \(65^\circ\)C, find \(k\), to three decimal places.
questions.answer: \(65=22+63e^{-8k}\Rightarrow e^{-8k}=\frac{43}{63}\approx0.6825\). Taking natural logs: \(-8k\approx-0.3819\), so \(k\approx0.0477\).

questions.q: A metal rod at \(200^\circ\)C cools in air at \(25^\circ\)C, with cooling constant \(k=0.03\) per minute. Find its temperature after 15 minutes, to the nearest degree.

This question has three parts. A tank contains \(300\) litres of brine with \(10\) kg of dissolved salt. Fresh water flows in at \(6\) litres/minute, and the well-mixed solution flows out at the same rate, keeping the volume constant. Let \(S(t)\) be the mass of salt (kg) at time \(t\) minutes. (a) Explain why \(\frac{dS}{dt}=-\frac{S}{50}\). (b) Solve this differential equation for \(S(t)\), given \(S(0)=10\). (c) Find how long it takes for the salt content to drop to \(2\) kg, to the nearest minute.
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: a mixing tank
questions.answer: (a) Since the incoming water carries no salt, salt only leaves, at a rate equal to concentration times outflow: \(\frac{S}{300}\times6=\frac{S}{50}\) kg/min, so \(\frac{dS}{dt}=-\frac{S}{50}\). (b) Separate: \(\frac{dS}{S}=-\frac{dt}{50}\). Integrate: \(\ln S=-\frac{t}{50}+C\), so \(S=Ae^{-t/50}\). Using \(S(0)=10\): \(A=10\). Solution: \(S(t)=10e^{-t/50}\). (c) \(2=10e^{-t/50}\Rightarrow e^{-t/50}=0.2\Rightarrow-\frac{t}{50}=\ln0.2\approx-1.6094\Rightarrow t\approx80\) minutes.
questions.explanation: (a) Since the incoming water carries no salt, salt only leaves, at a rate equal to concentration times outflow: \(\frac{S}{300}\times6=\frac{S}{50}\) kg/min, so \(\frac{dS}{dt}=-\frac{S}{50}\). (b) Separate: \(\frac{dS}{S}=-\frac{dt}{50}\). Integrate: \(\ln S=-\frac{t}{50}+C\), so \(S=Ae^{-t/50}\). Using \(S(0)=10\): \(A=10\). Solution: \(S(t)=10e^{-t/50}\). (c) \(2=10e^{-t/50}\Rightarrow e^{-t/50}=0.2\Rightarrow-\frac{t}{50}=\ln0.2\approx-1.6094\Rightarrow t\approx80\) minutes.

questions.q: Given \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x}{y} \) and \( y(0)=8 \) (with \( y>0 \)), find \( y(15) \).
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. Separating variables: \( y\,dy=x\,dx\Rightarrow y^2=x^2+C \). Using \( y(0)=8 \): \( C=(8)^2=64 \). At \( x=15 \): \( y^2=(15)^2+64=289\Rightarrow y=17 \). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Separating variables: \( y\,dy=x\,dx\Rightarrow y^2=x^2+C \). Using \( y(0)=8 \): \( C=(8)^2=64 \). At \( x=15 \): \( y^2=(15)^2+64=289\Rightarrow y=17 \). [M1][A1]

questions.q: Solve the first-order linear differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x}y = 4x\) for \(x > 0\), given the initial condition \(y(1) = 2\).
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: a mixing tank
questions.answer: 1. Identify \(P(x) = \frac{2}{x}\) and \(Q(x) = 4x\). 2. Calculate the integrating factor \(\mu(x)\): \(\mu(x) = \exp\left( \int \frac{2}{x}\,dx \right) = e^{2\ln x} = e^{\ln(x^2)} = x^2.\) 3. Multiply through by \(x^2\): \(x^2\frac{dy}{dx} + 2x y = 4x^3 \Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx}[x^2 y] = 4x^3.\) 4. Integrate both sides: \(x^2 y = \int 4x^3\,dx = x^4 + C.\) 5. Apply \(y(1) = 2\): \((1)^2(2) = 1^4 + C \Rightarrow 2 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = 1.\) 6. Explicit solution: \(y = \frac{x^4 + 1}{x^2} = x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2}.\)
questions.explanation: 1. Identify \(P(x) = \frac{2}{x}\) and \(Q(x) = 4x\). 2. Calculate the integrating factor \(\mu(x)\): \(\mu(x) = \exp\left( \int \frac{2}{x}\,dx \right) = e^{2\ln x} = e^{\ln(x^2)} = x^2.\) 3. Multiply through by \(x^2\): \(x^2\frac{dy}{dx} + 2x y = 4x^3 \Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx}[x^2 y] = 4x^3.\) 4. Integrate both sides: \(x^2 y = \int 4x^3\,dx = x^4 + C.\) 5. Apply \(y(1) = 2\): \((1)^2(2) = 1^4 + C \Rightarrow 2 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = 1.\) 6. Explicit solution: \(y = \frac{x^4 + 1}{x^2} = x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2}.\)

questions.q: Solve the second-order homogeneous linear differential equation \(y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0\) satisfying initial conditions \(y(0) = 1\) and \(y'(0) = 3\).
questions.answer: 1. Write the characteristic equation: \(m^2 - 5m + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (m - 2)(m - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow m_1 = 2, \; m_2 = 3.\) 2. General solution: \(y(x) = A e^{2x} + B e^{3x}.\) 3. Derivative: \(y'(x) = 2A e^{2x} + 3B e^{3x}.\) 4. Apply initial conditions: \(y(0) = 1 \Rightarrow A + B = 1\). \(y'(0) = 3 \Rightarrow 2A + 3B = 3\). Multiply first equation by 2: \(2A + 2B = 2\). Subtract from second: \(B = 1\). Then \(A = 1 - 1 = 0\). Particular Solution: \(y(x) = e^{3x}.\)
questions.explanation: 1. Write the characteristic equation: \(m^2 - 5m + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (m - 2)(m - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow m_1 = 2, \; m_2 = 3.\) 2. General solution: \(y(x) = A e^{2x} + B e^{3x}.\) 3. Derivative: \(y'(x) = 2A e^{2x} + 3B e^{3x}.\) 4. Apply initial conditions: \(y(0) = 1 \Rightarrow A + B = 1\). \(y'(0) = 3 \Rightarrow 2A + 3B = 3\). Multiply first equation by 2: \(2A + 2B = 2\). Subtract from second: \(B = 1\). Then \(A = 1 - 1 = 0\). Particular Solution: \(y(x) = e^{3x}.\)

The first three terms of a geometric progression are given by \(u_1 = 3k - 2, \quad u_2 = k + 2, \quad u_3 = k - 2,\) where \(k\) is a real constant. Given that the infinite geometric series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_n\) converges, find the sum to infinity, \(S_\infty\).
questions.answer: Step 1: Set up the common ratio property of a geometric sequence. Since the terms form a geometric progression, the ratio between consecutive terms must be equal: \(\frac{u_2}{u_1} = \frac{u_3}{u_2} \Rightarrow u_2^2 = u_1 u_3\) Step 2: Substitute the expressions in terms of \(k\): \((k + 2)^2 = (3k - 2)(k - 2)\) \(k^2 + 4k + 4 = 3k^2 - 8k + 4\) Step 3: Solve the quadratic equation for \(k\): \(2k^2 - 12k = 0 \Rightarrow 2k(k - 6) = 0\) Thus, \(k = 0\) or \(k = 6\). Step 4: Apply the convergence criterion \(|r| < 1\): - If \(k = 0\): \(u_1 = -2\), \(u_2 = 2\), and \(r = \frac{2}{-2} = -1\). Since \(|r| = |-1| = 1 ot< 1\), the infinite series diverges. - If \(k = 6\): \(u_1 = 3(6) - 2 = 16\), \(u_2 = 6 + 2 = 8\), and \(r = \frac{8}{16} = \frac{1}{2}\). Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{2} < 1\), the series converges. Step 5: Calculate the sum to infinity \(S_\infty\): \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{16}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{16}{\frac{1}{2}} = 32\) Common Misconceptions: - Choice B (\(-1\)) arises from incorrectly assuming the \(k = 0\) case converges and evaluating \(\frac{-2}{1 - (-1)} = -1\). - Choice C (\(\frac{32}{3}\)) arises from using the incorrect formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 + r}\). - Choice D (\(16\)) confuses the sum to infinity with the first term \(a\).
questions.explanation: Step 1: Set up the common ratio property of a geometric sequence. Since the terms form a geometric progression, the ratio between consecutive terms must be equal: \(\frac{u_2}{u_1} = \frac{u_3}{u_2} \Rightarrow u_2^2 = u_1 u_3\) Step 2: Substitute the expressions in terms of \(k\): \((k + 2)^2 = (3k - 2)(k - 2)\) \(k^2 + 4k + 4 = 3k^2 - 8k + 4\) Step 3: Solve the quadratic equation for \(k\): \(2k^2 - 12k = 0 \Rightarrow 2k(k - 6) = 0\) Thus, \(k = 0\) or \(k = 6\). Step 4: Apply the convergence criterion \(|r| < 1\): - If \(k = 0\): \(u_1 = -2\), \(u_2 = 2\), and \(r = \frac{2}{-2} = -1\). Since \(|r| = |-1| = 1 ot< 1\), the infinite series diverges. - If \(k = 6\): \(u_1 = 3(6) - 2 = 16\), \(u_2 = 6 + 2 = 8\), and \(r = \frac{8}{16} = \frac{1}{2}\). Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{2} < 1\), the series converges. Step 5: Calculate the sum to infinity \(S_\infty\): \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{16}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{16}{\frac{1}{2}} = 32\) Common Misconceptions: - Choice B (\(-1\)) arises from incorrectly assuming the \(k = 0\) case converges and evaluating \(\frac{-2}{1 - (-1)} = -1\). - Choice C (\(\frac{32}{3}\)) arises from using the incorrect formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 + r}\). - Choice D (\(16\)) confuses the sum to infinity with the first term \(a\).

questions.q: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function given by \(f(x) = \left\{ k(4 - x^2), 0 \leq x \leq 2, ; 0, \mathrm{otherwise,} \right.\) where \(k\) is a constant. Find the value of \(k\).
questions.answer: For \(f(x)\) to be a valid probability density function, the total area under the curve must equal 1: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, dx = 1\) Substitute the non-zero definition of \(f(x)\): \(\int_0^2 k(4 - x^2) \, dx = 1\) Factor out the constant \(k\) and integrate term by term: \(k \left[ 4x - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^2 = 1\) Evaluate at the upper and lower limits: \(k \left( \left( 4(2) - \frac{2^3}{3} \right) - 0 \right) = 1\) \(k \left( 8 - \frac{8}{3} \right) = 1\) \(k \left( \frac{16}{3} \right) = 1 \Rightarrow k = \frac{3}{16}\) Common errors include: - Integrating \(x^2\) as \(x^2\) or dividing by 2 instead of 3, leading to \(k = \frac{1}{4}\). - Integrating over \([-2, 2]\) instead of \([0, 2]\), which gives double the integral and results in \(k = \frac{3}{8}\). - Evaluating the integral correctly as \(\frac{16}{3}\) but forgetting to invert to solve for \(k\), yielding \(\frac{16}{3}\).
